articles.title: FYI: OpenAI "spend limits" aren't always limits
articles.title_ja: FYI: OpenAI "spend limits" aren't always limits
articles.summary_ja:
Title: FYI: OpenAI "spend limits" aren't always limits
HN text: My OpenAI API key got hacked this morning, and the bot started using my key for something in Chinese. "No worries," I thought, "I have a $30 spend limit setup." When I came back to my desk an hour later, I had $285 in unauthorized charges. As it turns out, OpenAI will let you create a spend limit _without_ checking "enforce spend limit." If you don't check enforce, it's meaningless. So even though my account showed that I had a $30 spend limit, it still let the hacker blow right past it by hundreds of dollars. I've submitted a dispute, but wanted to let other people know so it doesn't bite you, too. You can check your spend limits at https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/limits

Title: Random-bench / Benchmarks are Astrology for LLMs
Article title: Isaac Fisher - Blog

Article text:
random-bench / Benchmarks are Astrology for LLMs
Benchmarks are a hot topic lately. Every other week, some new model has achieved some incredible number on a benchmark I've never seen before. I, personally, am tired of the benchflation pioneered by certain reckless frontier AI companies. Although they're often marketing nonsense, leakage is probably real, and “rogue” agent cheating is more common than ever, there's a certain mystical appeal to benchmarks, and they do generally signal improvement, give or take. While they may not be perfect (or, in some cases, meaningful in real-world contexts at all), you can learn quite a bit about models from their performances on even arbitrary tasks.
